title: Continuity & Fallbacks Strategy Eval - Aurora Health
summary: Discovery focused on reliability posture for a HIPAA-adjacent healthcare product. Main concerns: how Redwood handles regional outages, transparent fallbacks between Hosted/Dedicated/Private, what SLA guarantees look like, and encryption / audit requirements for PHI-adjacent telemetry. Customer is evaluating a pilot with Dedicated or VPC Private, wants a multi-region continuity plan and a short benchmark to validate tail latency under failover.
topics: Fallback policies and automatic model variant routing
Multi-region routing and geo failover options
Data residency, KMS/HSM, and audit logs
Pilot scope and success criteria (latency, cost, throughput)
next_steps: Redwood to share Private deployment security pack and SOC2 artifacts [link: redwood-security-pack.pdf]
SE to run 2-hour benchmark script using Aurora sample prompts and share latency distribution report
Schedule follow-up technical deep dive to map network topology for VPC peering (week of Aug 18)
Redwood AE to send preliminary Dedicated pricing and pilot contract template
action_items: Maya Chen - Send security pack and SOC2 summary by 2025-08-07
Ravi Patel - Run benchmark with 10k tokens/day load and provide p50/p90/p99 latency by 2025-08-11
Jonas Rivera (Aurora) - Provide sample prompts + target QPS and allowed regions by 2025-08-08
Priya Desai (Aurora) - Confirm encryption/KMS requirements and compliance controls by 2025-08-12
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2025-08-05
Start: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Carlos (Redwood CS), Sara (CTO - Aurora), Jonas (Platform), Priya (Security), Ethan (SRE)

Summary: quick discovery on continuity strategy and fallback behaviors for a regulated healthcare use case. They want to understand how Redwood keeps apps online during infra incidents and how to prove it with a short pilot.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Sara (Aurora): Sara here.
[00:08] Jonas (Aurora): Jonas.
[00:09] Priya (Aurora): Priya.
[00:10] Ethan (Aurora): Ethan.
[00:12] Maya: Great, so goal for today, walk through our reliability knobs — fallback policies, multi-region routing, and what an SLA looks like, and then figure next steps for a pilot. Ravi will handle the deep dive.
[00:25] Ravi (Redwood): Hi all, quick context: Aurora said they are HIPAA-adjacent, so prescriptive around egress, KMS, audit logs. We'll assume PHI won't be in prompts but metadata might be sensitive. Is that correct, Priya?
[00:38] Priya: Correct, mostly PHI-adjacent, but logs and traces must be encrypted and auditable. We also have residency requirements, we prefer US-only regions for now.
[00:47] Ravi: Got it. On the runtime side, Redwood supports hosted, dedicated, and private/VPC. From a continuity pov we have multiple levers: model variant fallbacks, routing by policy (latency vs region vs cost), and multi-region replication of the serving pool.
[01:05] Jonas: Quick question — if a region goes down, do you failover to another region with the same model, or do you downgrade to a smaller model to preserve latency?
[01:13] Ravi: Both are possible — we have policies. Typical config is: 1) primary route to local region, 2) fallback to warm standby region with the same model variant if capacity allows, 3) if the same variant isn't available we can route to a quantized or 8-bit variant to keep throughput up. The decision can be per-customer, per-route.
[01:34] Sara: What's the expected tail latency impact when you do region failover? I'm worried about p99s spiking.
[01:40] Ravi: During DNS/policy shift you'll see a transient p99 increase for in-flight requests — on average we see p99 increase for a few seconds to low 10s of seconds while caches and KV states warm. We mitigate with active warm-standby pools and prefix-KV cache hydration. But yes, there is a tail bump.
[02:05] Ethan: How do you handle KV cache when requests land in a different region? Do you replicate KV caches?
[02:11] Ravi: We don't replicate KV across regions in real-time for privacy/consistency reasons. Instead we use a two-pronged approach: 1) prefix caching — keep common prefixes hot on standby nodes, 2) best-effort async prefetch for recent sessions. For strict session stickiness we recommend session routing with global LB + consistent hashing.
[02:35] Priya: That makes sense. From compliance we need every access to be logged with user id, timestamp, and reason. Can Redwood export those logs to our SIEM or S3?
[02:45] Carlos (Redwood CS): Yes — audit logs can stream to customer S3 buckets or to SIEM via syslog/forwarding. Logs can be encrypted with customer KMS keys. We can also provide immutable event records for a retention window — configuration is per-customer.
[03:02] Priya: Good, and HSM support?
[03:05] Maya: We integrate with major KMS providers, and for Dedicated/Private we can support HSM-backed keys depending on deployment. We'll include details in the security pack.
[03:16] Jonas: On routing: is that managed by Redwood control plane or does Aurora need to setup a global LB?
[03:22] Ravi: Redwood control plane supports smart routing policies. You can say prefer-region, allowed-regions, cost-tier, or latency-first. For Private/VPC mode we do a control-plane to dataplane handshake; often customers front the service with their own LB for additional routing control, but it's not required.
[03:40] Sara: SLA — can you give us a sense for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private? We're mostly concerned with guaranteed uptime and latency SLOs for our production traffic.
[03:49] Maya: Hosted has best-effort SLOs published — we provide transparency on latency distributions, but SLA-backed guarantees live in Dedicated and Enterprise Private where we do capacity commitments and uptime SLAs. Typical Dedicated SLA is 99.9% with latency targets negotiated by region and model family. For Private we can do tighter SLAs if it's a managed deployment with committed ops.
[04:14] Priya: If we need 99.95 for a critical API, is that achievable?
[04:18] Maya: Potentially, but it depends on traffic profile and architecture. Achieving 99.95 may require cross-region active-active, more reserved capacity, and tighter monitoring/alerting. We can model that during the pilot.
[04:31] Ethan: Speaking of pilot, what does Redwood usually run to validate continuity?
[04:35] Ravi: We do a failover drill: run a synthetic workload at target QPS in primary region, then simulate regional outage or throttle capacity and verify fallback behavior — measure p50/p90/p99 over the window. We also run a KV-warmup pass to mimic session state. We aim for a 2-4 hour run for initial validation.
[04:55] Jonas: Cost — how much does warm-standby typically add?
[04:58] Maya: Warm-standby is a spectrum — you can keep minimal hot nodes (cheaper) or full standby (more expensive). Typical delta is 10-30% on top of active capacity depending on model size and replication factor. We'll provide example math in the pricing sheet.
[05:15] Sara: For our compliance team, we need a clear escalation playbook for incidents. Do you provide runbooks and paging integrations?
[05:22] Carlos: Yes — Redwood provides operational runbooks, and we can integrate with PagerDuty/Slack/Teams. For Dedicated/Private we can also provide on-call escalation with an SRE retainer as an add-on.
[05:36] Priya: We also want to ensure that during failover we don't leak PII into logs that are forwarded externally.
[05:42] Ravi: We'll scrub or mask prompt data per policy before any external exports. For Private deployments you can keep logs entirely on-prem or in your VPC.
[05:50] Sara: Demo question — can you show the routing policy UI or is that console-only?
[05:54] Maya: We can show it; it's in the Console. For this call we can point to screenshots and then schedule a live demo.
[06:02] Jonas: One technical thing — how do you ensure model compatibility when fallback goes to a different variant? Some of our prompts expect structured output, so we don't want behavior regressions.
[06:13] Ravi: Great point. Redwood supports behavioral constraints and eval hooks — you can configure canary policies that only fallback to variants that have passed a specified eval set. If a variant regresses on the eval prompts we will not route to it automatically; instead we'd fallback to an alternate standby or signal an error depending on policy.
[06:34] Priya: That sounds useful. Will the fallback decision be visible in logs for auditing?
[06:38] Carlos: Yes — every routing decision is recorded with reason, timestamp, and selected variant. Those can be exported for audits.
[06:45] Sara: Network peering — if we go Private, how does peering work with our VPC?
[06:50] Ravi: Two options: 1) VPC peering / PrivateLink-style endpoints where traffic stays inside the cloud backbone, or 2) customer fronting LB with mTLS to Redwood connectors. We'll map whichever fits your security posture.
[07:03] Ethan: Does Redwood support active-active across regions or is it active-standby?
[07:07] Ravi: Both models are supported. Active-active requires careful session routing and KV strategy. For low-latency access, active-active with region-affinity routing and consistent hashing is recommended. Active-standby is simpler operationally.
[07:22] Jonas: Any known gotchas with consistent hashing and session stickiness when using CDN or external load balancers?
[07:27] Ravi: Yes — if you have a CDN that terminates and re-shuffles client IPs, you might break stickiness. Use a consistent token in the request headers or rely on session IDs for hashing to avoid dependency on client IP.
[07:40] Maya: Quick interjection — Priya, any non-negotiable compliance items we should note for the pilot?
[07:45] Priya: Auditability, KMS with customer-managed keys, and US-only residency for logs and backups. Also need a contract clause for breach notification within 48 hours.
[07:55] Maya: Noted — we'll flag those in the security pack and contract template.
[08:00] Jonas: On the benchmark: our target is 500 QPS at 50 tokens avg per request with p99 under 600ms. Is that realistic?
[08:09] Ravi: For certain model families and Dedicated pools yes; for large unquantized models p99 600ms is aggressive at 500 QPS. We can get closer with model quantization + batching and tuned kernels. We'll use your sample prompts to validate.
[08:25] Sara: Are there any blackout windows for maintenance that could affect the pilot?
[08:29] Carlos: For Dedicated customers we schedule maint windows with notice. For Hosted we do rolling updates but inform via status and can set maintenance windows for Private. We'll include maintenance policy in the docs.
[08:42] Ethan: Incident tolerance — can Redwood do automated rollback to previous model if new rollout causes regression?
[08:47] Ravi: Yes, rollouts support canary evaluation, automatic rollback on regression thresholds, and traffic shadowing for validation.
[08:56] Priya: How granular are the alerts? We want alerting on error rate, latency, and model regression metrics.
[09:02] Carlos: You can set per-route alerts. We ship metrics to Prometheus pushgateway or to cloud metrics; alert on p50/p90/p99, error rate, and eval drift.
[09:14] Jonas: For the pilot, do we need a full Dedicated cluster or can we start with a small Private connector?
[09:19] Maya: Often customers start with a small Dedicated pilot or a Private control-plane with a lightweight on-prem dataplane connector. Depends on how isolated you want workloads. We'll propose options.
[09:31] Sara: Walk me through a hypothetical outage: region A fails, traffic flips to region B, we see increased costs and slight latency — who's responsible for failover ops?
[09:40] Maya: Operationally, Redwood automates routing and fallback. For Dedicated we own the serving plane and coordinate; for Private we provide tooling and automation but your infra team controls peering and routing decisions if you choose. We'll clarify responsibilities in the SLA.
[09:57] Ethan: Any performance regressions when moving from a 32-bit model to 8-bit quantized fallback?
[10:02] Ravi: Behavior can shift — quantized models sometimes hallucinate more or change tokenization boundaries. That's why we recommend eval gating before automatic fallback. If structured outputs are critical, disable automated fallback to different families.
[10:18] Sara: Ok that's important. We'll want that in writing.
[10:21] Maya: We'll include config snippets and the default behavior in the pilot doc.
[10:25] Jonas: One last technical — can we shadow prod traffic to Redwood without affecting latency?
[10:30] Ravi: Yes — traffic shadowing is supported; it runs asynchronously and doesn't add client-visible latency. We'll need throttling controls and sampling to limit costs.
[10:40] Priya: For log retention, what's the default and can we set it to 1 year?
[10:44] Carlos: Defaults vary; we can configure retention windows per-customer up to multi-year if you provision lifecycle policies on the S3 side.
[10:52] Maya: Let's capture next steps.
[10:55] Sara: Confirming — we want the security pack, a pricing estimate for warm-standby, and a benchmark run on our prompts.
[11:03] Maya: Correct. We'll send the security pack and pricing. Ravi will run the benchmark with your sample prompts after Jonas uploads them.
[11:12] Jonas: I'll upload the prompt set and expected outputs to the shared folder by Friday.
[11:16] Priya: I'll review the security pack and call out any gaps.
[11:20] Maya: Great — we'll reconvene after the benchmark results, and plan the technical deep dive for VPC peering. Thanks everyone.
[11:26] Sara: Thanks all.

[11:30] End meeting
notes: Customer is HIPAA-adjacent; US-only residency requested
Pilot target: 500 QPS, p99 target 600ms (to be validated)
Recommended pilot: 2-4 hour failover drill + KV warmup
